passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Deepika, 12 August
Trisha got 9 out of 25 in the science test again. When I gave the paper back, she said, "You always give me low marks, ma'am. Riddhi is lucky, you like her." I asked how she had studied. She said she hadn't, because "it doesn't matter, it depends on your mood". She says this after almost every test. On the one test she did revise for, the plants chapter in July, she got 21, but when I reminded her, she said the questions were "just easy that day". I am worried she has stopped trying.
What I did next: I asked her to revise one short topic with me on Wednesday, and we will put the two marks side by side to see what changed.

qa.q: What did Trisha get on the plants chapter test she revised for?
Why does Trisha say the marks depend on the teacher's mood?
qa.a: Believing results come from outside feels easier than linking them to her own preparation; it also spares her the worry that revising might not help.

qa.q: What choice by Deepika could help Trisha see the link to effort?
qa.a: Revising one short topic together and putting the marks side by side, so Trisha sees for herself what preparation changes.

qa.q: How might Riddhi feel if she heard she was only "lucky"?
qa.a: Riddhi might feel her own hard work had been dismissed, and a little hurt at being called the teacher's favourite.

grounding: A child explains low marks as the teacher's mood or luck and never connects them to preparation.

passage: In the one-room school at Khandala, the spelling results were read out every Saturday. Ganga, who was nine, got four out of ten again. "The teacher reads too fast when it's my turn," she told her neighbour Farhan on the walk home, kicking a stone. "And she gives the hard words to me. It's bad luck." Farhan, eleven, said nothing for a while. He had seen her spelling list lying under the bangle box all week, never opened. "Last month you practised with your Ammi and got nine," he said. Ganga shrugged. "That was easy-words day." She walked faster, ahead of him, swinging her bag.

qa.q: What did Ganga score in the spelling test?
Why does Ganga call it bad luck rather than practice?
qa.a: Blaming the teacher's speed and the hard words protects her from feeling she could have done better, and makes practising seem useless.

qa.q: What could help Ganga link her marks to practice?
qa.a: Practising the list with her Ammi again before the next Saturday and comparing the scores, so she can see the difference herself.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Ganga walks ahead of him?
qa.a: Farhan may feel awkward or brushed off, since he was only pointing out something true and she doesn't want to hear it.

grounding: A child in a village school blames spelling marks on the teacher and luck, ignoring the unopened list.

subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
passage: Rafael came home from school in Seville and threw his maths test on the kitchen table. Four out of ten. "Señora Ortiz hates me," he said. "She was in a bad mood, so she marked hard." His older brother Javier, sixteen, picked up the paper. "Did you practise the fractions she gave you?" "What's the point? Last time I got six and I didn't practise either. It's luck." "Lucía got ten." "Because she sits at the front. Teachers like the front." Javier turned the page over. Every wrong answer was a fraction sum from the practice sheet, still folded in Rafael's bag, blank. Rafael didn't look. He was already switching on the TV, sure that next week would depend on Señora Ortiz's mood too.

qa.q: What mark did Rafael get on the maths test?
Why does blaming Señora Ortiz's mood feel right to Rafael?
qa.a: It spares him the idea that practice matters; if marks are luck or mood, a low score isn't his fault and skipping the sheet costs nothing.

qa.q: What could Javier try to help Rafael see the link between preparation and marks?
qa.a: Sit with him to do the blank practice sheet, point out that the wrong answers were exactly those sums, and compare next week's result.

qa.q: What might Javier be thinking as he turns the page over?
qa.a: Javier probably sees the pattern clearly, wrong answers matching the blank sheet, and may feel frustrated that his younger brother won't look.

grounding: A child blames the teacher's mood and luck for low marks and never connects them with his skipped practice.

subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
passage: At the government school in Indore, the weekly spelling test came back on Friday. Gautam, nine, had six out of twenty. He shoved the paper into his desk. "Nikita Ma'am gives me the hardest words," he told his bench-mate. "She reads fast when it's my row." Nikita Ma'am, walking past, heard. She crouched beside him. "Gautam, which words did you practise this week?" He shrugged. "None. It doesn't matter. Some weeks I'm lucky, some weeks not." "Last month you practised with your sister and got fourteen, remember?" Gautam frowned. "That was a good day." He picked at the edge of the desk. It had not occurred to him that the good day and the practice might be the same thing.

qa.q: What did Gautam score on the spelling test?
Why does Gautam call the fourteen 'a good day'?
qa.a: Gautam feels discouraged and sure results come from luck or Ma'am's speed, so even his best score seems like chance rather than something his practice caused.

qa.q: What could Nikita Ma'am do next to help Gautam link practice and marks?
qa.a: Start a simple weekly chart of words practised and marks, so Gautam can see the practice and the fourteen side by side.

qa.q: How might Nikita Ma'am feel hearing that she reads fast for his row?
qa.a: She may feel a little stung but more concerned, seeing that Gautam believes his marks depend on her rather than on his preparation.

grounding: A child says the teacher gives him hard words and that marks are luck, never linking results with practice.
